0.title: Two Thousand Years of Grace
0.essay:
Church history is not a human story in which God occasionally appears. It is God’s story, unfolding through human instruments — frail, fallible, sometimes faithless — yet preserved and carried forward by the one who said, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

A promise tested

Two thousand years have tested that promise in every way imaginable: persecution, heresy, compromise, corruption, apostasy and worldly power. The promise has held.

To study church history is to be humbled and awed at once. Humbled, because the church has often been its own worst enemy: the Crusades, the Inquisition, the complicity of German churches under National Socialism, the prosperity gospel of our own day. Awed, because through all of it God has preserved a people for his name. In every dark century and every persecuted corner of the world there have been those who held the gospel, sang the psalms, broke the bread and passed the faith to the next generation. The gates of hell have pushed hard. They have not prevailed.

The questions we ask

This study traces the story through eight great movements, from the fire of Pentecost to the global church of the twenty-first century, always asking: what was God doing? What can we learn? What must we hold, and what must we repent of?

Its governing conviction is Reformed. The church is most faithful when it is most tethered to the word of God alone, and most corrupt when it puts tradition, experience or power in the place of Scripture.

The chapters

The Apostolic Age (c. AD 30–100); The Early Fathers and the Creeds (100–451); Augustine and the Western Church (354–604); The Medieval Church (600–1500); The Reformation (1517–1564); Post-Reformation and Puritanism (1560–1700); The Great Awakenings (1700–1850); and The Modern Church (1850 to the present).

1.title: The Apostolic Age (c. AD 30–100)
1.essay:
The church was born in fire. On the Day of Pentecost, fifty days after the resurrection, the Holy Spirit fell on the disciples in Jerusalem and three thousand people were added in a single day. A frightened band of a hundred and twenty became, within decades, a movement stretching from Jerusalem to Rome.

Born of the Spirit

No human organisation, political movement or philosophical school has ever grown so fast from such unpromising beginnings. The church was not a human institution that gradually took on religious colouring. It was born by a direct act of the Holy Spirit, in fulfilment of Jesus’ promise (John 14–16) and Joel’s prophecy (Acts 2:17–21). It is the creation of God’s word and Spirit, called into being by the gospel and sustained by the same Spirit. That is why no power on earth can finally destroy it.

The Pentecost church was marked by four things: “they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). They have been the marks of a healthy church in every generation since. Where the apostolic teaching — now the New Testament — is central, where real community exists, where the Lord’s Supper is kept and where prayer is the atmosphere, there is a church in the New Testament sense. The church did not invent these marks; they were given at its birth.

Paul and the nations

After Jesus himself, the apostle Paul is the most consequential figure in Christian history. Three missionary journeys, thirteen letters and a theology of grace shaped Augustine, Luther, Calvin and every reformation since. Paul understood before anyone else that the gospel was not a Jewish sect but a message for every nation. His letter to the Romans is the most sustained argument in the New Testament, a cathedral of grace. When he died in Rome under Nero — beheaded, by tradition, around AD 67 — he had planted churches from Antioch to Rome, longed to reach Spain, and laid the theological foundations the church would return to for two millennia.

The fall of Jerusalem

The Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 was the most shattering event of the first century. The temple was burned and the city razed, and Josephus says over a million Jews died. For Jewish Christianity it was the end of an era. For the Gentile church it confirmed that the new covenant had fulfilled the old: the temple made with hands had given way to the temple of Christ’s body (John 2:21).

John on Patmos

The last surviving apostle, exiled to a prison island in the Aegean, wrote the last book of the Bible. Revelation is a pastoral letter to seven persecuted churches, clothed in the language of Jewish apocalyptic — a form suited to saying what could not be said openly under imperial surveillance. Stripped of its imagery, its message is simple and electrifying: the Lamb wins. Caesar is not lord; Jesus is. The beast that seems to rule the world is already defeated. Hold fast. John on Patmos is the image of the church in every age of persecution: stripped of everything except the vision of the risen Christ, and finding that it is enough.

The legacy: the New Testament

What the apostolic age left every later generation is irreplaceable: the New Testament. Its twenty-seven books are the norm by which every church, tradition and teacher is measured. The church did not create the canon; it recognised what God had inspired. And every church is apostolic to the degree that it submits to the apostles’ testimony — “the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3).

With the death of the last apostle, that deposit was complete. No new revelation is needed. This is not a limitation but a liberation: the church of every age has in the New Testament everything it needs to know God, be saved, live faithfully and die well. This is the root of the Reformation’s principle of Scripture alone.

Then and now

The early church grew not through political power, institutional prestige or cultural accommodation, but through a message the world thought foolish: a crucified and risen Jewish carpenter is Lord of all. The Roman Empire had every resource to crush it. Within three centuries the emperor himself would be baptised. Tertullian’s words proved prophetic: “the blood of Christians is seed.”

The church in the West is in numerical decline. The temptation is to update the message, soften the offence and accommodate the culture. The apostolic age answers that temptation directly. The church grew when it was most distinct from its culture, not when it was most similar. Paul was “not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16). Hold it, proclaim it and trust it.

For reflection

How healthy are the four marks of Acts 2:42 in your church? What does it mean for you that the apostolic deposit is complete? How does John’s vision on Patmos speak to Christians under pressure today?

2.title: The Early Fathers and the Creeds (AD 100–451)
2.essay:
The second and third centuries were the age of martyrs and apologists — those who died for the faith and those who defended it with pen and argument. Rome alternated between persecution and uneasy tolerance, and the church grew in both seasons. But the greater danger came from within.

The martyrs

Between Nero’s persecution in AD 64 and Constantine’s Edict of Milan in 313, the church lived under periodic threat of imperial violence. Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in Rome around 108, wrote seven letters to churches along his route. What strikes the reader is the longing: the eager desire to be with Christ, the willingness to be ground like wheat so that others might live. He was also the first writer outside the New Testament to call the church “catholic”, meaning universal, and he stressed the bishop’s role in keeping unity and sound doctrine.

Polycarp of Smyrna, burned at the stake in old age, refused to curse Christ: “Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?” Perpetua, a young noblewoman with a nursing baby, walked into the arena at Carthage in 203 rather than offer incense to the emperor. They were not exceptional Christians but ordinary believers who understood that Jesus is Lord and Caesar is not. Their courage is the church’s permanent inheritance, and its rebuke.

The church survived and grew because its gospel was true, because the Spirit was at work, and because its members loved one another in a way the pagan world found incomprehensible. Tertullian reported that pagans said of Christians, “See how they love one another.” The church grew as much by its life as by its arguments.

The heresies

Gnosticism, Marcionism and Arianism each tried, in its own way, to have Christianity without the incarnation, without the full deity of Christ, or without the scandal of the cross. Arius taught that the Son was the highest of created beings — divine, exalted, worthy of worship, but not truly God. If he was right, there is no salvation, because only God can save. A creature, however exalted, cannot bear the sins of the world or unite humanity with God.

Nicaea and Athanasius

The Council of Nicaea in 325, called by the Emperor Constantine, is the hinge of the period. It declared what the Scriptures teach: the Son is of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father. One word stood between the church and a Christ who could not save.

Athanasius grasped this with total clarity and fought for it with his career, his freedom and very nearly his life. Exiled five times by emperors who favoured Arius, he returned five times — “Athanasius against the world”. The world blinked first. The creed that came from Nicaea, refined at Constantinople in 381, remains the ecumenical statement of Christian orthodoxy: “God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father.”

Chalcedon

If Nicaea settled Christ’s full deity, the Council of Chalcedon in 451 settled his full humanity. Against those who said he had only a divine nature and those who divided him into two persons, Chalcedon declared that the one Christ is fully God and fully man — two natures, one person, without confusion or separation. The church, under pressure from every side, held together what Scripture teaches and salvation requires. To be orthodox is to confess the Christ of Chalcedon: truly God, truly man, one Lord.

The creeds

The creeds are not additions to Scripture but summaries of it, forged in controversy. The Apostles’ Creed, second-century in origin and in its present form by the seventh century, is the baptismal confession of the Western church. The Nicene Creed is affirmed by virtually every branch of Christianity. Reformed theology has always embraced them as accurate summaries of biblical truth, while insisting that Scripture alone is the final authority. The creeds serve Scripture; they do not rule it.

The church did not invent doctrine in this period; it clarified and defended what Scripture had always taught, saying as precisely as it could what the Bible says about the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That is legitimate development — not new revelation, but careful explanation of the faith once delivered.

The cost of truth

Nicene faith cost Athanasius exile after exile; the faith of Chalcedon cost some their careers and some their lives. Truth is never free. Jude’s call “to contend for the faith” (Jude 3) is not a call to theological aggression but to theological courage: holding what the church has always held, against the pressure of the moment, at personal cost if necessary.

The great heresies have never died; they have only changed clothes. Every generation produces its Arius, who says Christ is the highest but not truly God; its Marcion, who says the God of the Old Testament is not the God of the New; its Docetist, who says Jesus did not really suffer. The creeds are not museum pieces but weapons, forged in battle and still sharp. To know the Nicene Creed is to be armed against some of the most sophisticated errors of our own age.

For reflection

Why did one word, “homoousios”, matter so much? What does Polycarp’s answer say to you about loyalty to Christ? Read the Nicene Creed slowly. Which line means most to you, and which modern error does it answer?

3.title: Augustine and the Western Church (AD 354–604)
3.essay:
No figure in the history of the Western church casts a longer shadow than Augustine of Hippo (354–430). Theologian, bishop, pastor, controversialist and the most brilliant mind of his age, he shaped every major tradition that followed — Roman Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed.

A restless heart

Augustine was raised by a praying Christian mother, Monica, and a pagan father. He spent his young adulthood in restless intellectual and moral searching — through Manichaean dualism, through Neoplatonism, through a long relationship with a concubine and the son she bore him — until the grace of God arrested him in a garden in Milan in 386. The opening of his Confessions has become the most quoted sentence in Christian autobiography: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

The Confessions is often called the first autobiography in Western literature, and it is relentlessly honest. Augustine does not soften his past: the stolen pears, the concubinage, the years of rebellion against a God he half knew was there. What makes the book devastating is its honesty about how sin works: the will turned in on itself, unable to choose what it knows is good, needing grace from outside to set it free. His prayer “Grant what you command, and command what you will” is its heartbeat.

Monica prayed for him for years, through every wandering. A bishop she pleaded with told her, “It is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.” Augustine was converted at thirty-one, and Monica died the following year, at peace. For every praying parent the lesson is plain: God’s grace is not bound by time, and the prayers of the faithful are never lost.

Augustine and Pelagius

That prayer infuriated Pelagius, a British monk who taught that human beings have the natural capacity to choose God and live righteously, so that grace assists but does not begin the work. Augustine’s answer was total: sin has so corrupted the will that it cannot choose God without God’s prior, regenerating grace. We do not choose God and then receive grace; we receive grace and then, freely and joyfully, choose God. The battle between Augustine and Pelagius is the battle between every gospel-centred theology and every theology of self-improvement, and it is still fought in pulpits today.

Augustine’s most consequential teaching may be original sin: Adam’s sin corrupted not only his own nature but human nature as such, so that everyone born since inherits both its guilt and its corruption. That is not pessimism but realism, confirmed on every page of history, and it is the necessary backdrop for the gospel. If we are not radically corrupt, we do not need radical grace. The depth of the disease measures the glory of the cure.

Grace and predestination

Augustine is the father of the Reformed doctrine of grace. His mature teaching that God elects not on the basis of foreseen faith but by his own sovereign mercy is the direct ancestor of Calvin’s. Faith is not the cause of election but its fruit. He reached this not mainly by philosophy but through Scripture — above all Romans 9–11 — and through his own experience. He had not chosen God; God had chosen him, in a garden, in the middle of his rebellion, against the grain of his will. He never got over the grace of it.

He was emphatic that the renewed will is truly free. Grace does not make us puppets. But the unrenewed will is bound: it cannot choose what it does not desire, and it cannot desire God until God gives it a new heart. That is what the Reformers would later call sola gratia.

Two cities

After the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, Augustine wrote The City of God to explain the meaning of history. If “eternal Rome” can fall, what is permanent? Only the city of God. The earthly city — not a political state but all who love self to the contempt of God — will pass. The heavenly city — all who love God to the contempt of self — cannot fall, because it rests on God’s election and grace. The two are intermingled in history and indistinguishable to the eye, but at the last day they will be separated for ever.

Gregory the Great

Gregory I, bishop of Rome from 590 to 604, stands at the threshold of the medieval church. Deeply Augustinian on grace and a brilliant administrator, he made the papacy a major temporal power, sent Augustine of Canterbury to evangelise England, and wrote the Pastoral Rule, a guide for bishops on the care of souls that is among the wisest practical books in church history. He was Augustinian enough to preach grace, and institutional enough to build a structure that would one day need reformation.

Pelagius today

The Pelagian impulse is the default setting of the fallen heart: the assumption that with enough effort we can improve ourselves into God’s approval. Every self-help spirituality, every prosperity gospel, every “your best life now” Christianity is Pelagianism in modern dress. Augustine’s answer was Paul’s: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The Christian life begins and ends with grace, and its deepest experience is not pride in our progress but astonishment that God chose us at all.

For reflection

Where do you see Pelagius’s assumption in yourself or in the church today? How does the doctrine of original sin make grace more wonderful? What encouragement does Monica’s story give you as you pray for someone?

4.title: The Medieval Church (AD 600–1500)
4.essay:
The medieval period is the most misunderstood era of church history. Popular imagination pictures a thousand years of darkness before the light of the Renaissance and Reformation. The reality is more complex and more interesting.

What the medieval church gave

The medieval church preserved classical learning through the collapse of Rome, built the universities of Europe, produced some of the greatest theologians in history, and kept — however imperfectly — the structures of Christian civilisation across a continent.

One of its quiet miracles was the preservation of Scripture. While the empire collapsed and invasion, plague, war and famine swept Europe, monks in Ireland, Britain and the continent copied manuscripts by candlelight in cold scriptoria. They did not always understand what they copied, and they sometimes embellished or corrupted the text. But the word of God survived. When Erasmus prepared his Greek New Testament in 1516, he had manuscripts to work from because anonymous monks had spent their lives preserving them. God does not lose his word.

Anselm

Anselm of Canterbury’s Cur Deus Homo — “Why God Became Man” (1098) — is one of the most important books in Christian theology. He argued that sin is an infinite offence against God’s infinite honour, so only an infinite payment could satisfy divine justice. Only God can make such payment; only man ought to make it. Therefore God became man. His framework was feudal honour rather than legal penalty, but his instinct was right: the atonement is not first an example or a display of love but a satisfaction of divine justice. Calvin and the Reformers developed it into the doctrine of penal substitution.

Aquinas

Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was the greatest theologian of the Middle Ages and one of the most brilliant minds in the history of philosophy. His synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology in the Summa Theologiae shaped Roman Catholic theology decisively. The Reformed tradition’s relationship with him is complex. It appreciates his philosophical rigour, his Augustinian instincts on grace and his defence of natural law, while rejecting his division between nature and grace, his doctrine of transubstantiation and his understanding of faith and merit. Calvin read Aquinas carefully and disagreed with him carefully — the mark of a serious theologian.

The gospel buried

Yet the medieval church had lost something essential. Justification by faith alone, the beating heart of Augustine’s theology, was never formally denied, but it was buried under a system of merit, penance, indulgences, purgatory and the treasury of the saints, which stood between the sinner and the grace of God. The Bible was in Latin, out of reach of ordinary people. The church had become wealthy, politically powerful and theologically muddled.

The ordinary medieval believer — a French peasant, an English merchant, a German farmer — lived without the Bible in their own language and without assurance of salvation, performing religious duties out of fear of purgatory and hoping that enough pilgrimages, indulgences, prayers and penances might tip the scales. That is not the gospel; it is exactly what Paul opposed in Galatia. It is what Luther experienced as an Augustinian monk, doing everything the system required and finding no peace.

The corruption

At its lowest points — the Borgia papacy, the sale of indulgences, the brutality of the Crusades, the Inquisition — the medieval church is a sobering study in what happens when an institution substitutes power for the gospel. In the tenth and eleventh centuries the papacy was the plaything of Roman noble families; some popes were elected as children, some were murderers, some openly kept mistresses. The sale of church offices, clerical immorality and confusion about salvation had made the church in many places barely recognisable as the community born at Pentecost. This is not anti-Catholic polemic; Roman Catholic historians acknowledge it. The Reformation answered a real crisis that the medieval church itself had been unable to resolve.

The morning stars

By the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, voices from within were crying for reform. John Wycliffe, an Oxford theologian, argued for two things the medieval church found intolerable: the authority of Scripture over the church, and the right of ordinary people to read the Bible in their own language. He and his associates produced the first complete English Bible and sent out “poor priests”, the Lollards, to preach it. He died of a stroke in 1384; the Council of Constance later condemned him, dug up his bones and burned them.

Jan Hus, a Bohemian reformer inspired by Wycliffe, was burned at the stake in 1415 despite a promise of safe conduct. Luther, reading of his death a century later, wrote, “We are all Hussites without knowing it.” The Reformation did not appear from nowhere. It came because the word of God, even when suppressed, cannot be silenced for ever.

What are you doing with it?

The medieval period shows that God’s word cannot be destroyed. It was kept in Latin and guarded by an institution that did not always want ordinary people reading it. Yet it was copied, translated at the cost of lives, and, when the printing press came, erupted across Europe with unstoppable force. It belongs to the people God has called, and it will reach them.

We have what medieval believers could only dream of: the Bible in our own language, in many translations, on every device we own. The question the period puts to us is not “Do you have access to the word?” but “What are you doing with it?” The monk copying by candlelight had less than we do, and perhaps treasured it more. The recovery of the gospel always begins with the rediscovery of the Book.

For reflection

What do you owe to the unknown copyists of Scripture? How did a system of merit hide the gospel from ordinary people, and where might something similar happen today? How are you treasuring the Bible you have?

5.title: The Reformation (AD 1517–1564)
5.essay:
On 31 October 1517 an Augustinian monk posted ninety-five theses on the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, an academic invitation to debate the sale of indulgences. Within weeks, thanks to the printing press, copies had spread across Germany. Within months Martin Luther was the most famous man in Europe. Within a decade the Western church was permanently divided, and the gospel of justification by faith alone had been recovered.

Restorers, not revolutionaries

The Reformation is the most consequential event in Western Christianity since Nicaea. Its central discovery — or rather recovery — was the gospel itself: sinners are justified before God not by any work, merit or sacramental act, but by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, to the glory of God alone. It was what Paul taught in Romans and Galatians, what Augustine argued against Pelagius, and what the medieval church had buried. The Reformers were not revolutionaries but restorers, clearing the rubble from something ancient.

Luther

Luther’s breakthrough came through long, agonised wrestling with Romans 1:17. He had hated the phrase “the righteousness of God”, reading it as the standard by which God condemns sinners. Then it broke open: the righteousness of God is not the standard by which he judges us but the gift by which he saves us. “Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” That is the Reformation in a sentence. The righteousness that justifies is not ours but Christ’s, credited to us and received by faith alone. Everything Luther did afterwards — translating the Bible into German, reforming worship, writing the catechisms — flowed from the conviction that ordinary people should have direct access to the grace of God.

At the Diet of Worms in 1521, alone before the emperor with the power of the Holy Roman Empire arrayed against him, he refused to recant unless convinced by Scripture or plain reason: “Here I stand, I can do no other, so help me God.” He had read how Hus went to the fire a century before under a similar promise of safe conduct. He stood anyway. That is what Scripture alone looks like when it costs something.

Calvin

If Luther was the Reformation’s hammer, John Calvin was its architect. His Institutes of the Christian Religion, first published in 1536 when he was twenty-six and expanded until his death, is the most systematic exposition of Reformed theology ever written. His genius was not originality but clarity: he took the biblical theology Luther had recovered and built it into a coherent system — the sovereignty of God in salvation, the authority of Scripture, the church, the sacraments, church and state — with a rigour and pastoral care that made Geneva a refuge for Protestant exiles and a training ground for pastors sent back across Europe.

The five solas

The five solas sum up the Reformation’s achievement. Scripture alone is the final authority, not tradition, pope or council. Salvation is by grace alone, not partly by human merit. Justification is through faith alone, not faith plus works. Christ alone is mediator, not Christ plus Mary, saints or priests. And to God alone be the glory, not to human achievement or church institution.

Scripture alone does not make tradition, councils and confessions worthless. It makes them subordinate to Scripture and reformable by it: the church is always to be reformed according to the word of God. That is not a licence for individualism but a limit on institutional power.

Justification by faith alone — God declaring sinners righteous on the basis of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith, with no admixture of merit — is not an exaggeration of the gospel but its heart. Later Lutherans called it the article by which the church stands or falls; Calvin called it the main hinge on which religion turns. If our standing rests partly on our own righteousness, we have no assurance and no peace. If it rests entirely on Christ’s, we have everything, and are free to love God and neighbour without the terror of condemnation.

England and Scotland

The Reformation took different shapes in different places. In England it began as much for political as for theological reasons, in Henry VIII’s desire for an annulment, but Thomas Cranmer gave it theological substance, embedding Reformed theology in the Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552). John Knox, the fiery Scot trained under Calvin in Geneva, brought the Reformation to Scotland so thoroughly that Scottish Presbyterianism became arguably the most consistently Reformed national church in history. His prayers, it was said, frightened Mary Queen of Scots more than an army of ten thousand men.

Trent

Rome’s answer was the Council of Trent (1545–1563), which clarified and hardened Catholic doctrine against the Reformation. It formally anathematised those who taught justification by faith alone, set tradition alongside Scripture as an equal authority, and affirmed transubstantiation and the sacrificial nature of the Mass. In one sense Trent was a real reform: it cleaned up clerical abuses and raised standards of education and conduct. But it deliberately excluded the recovery of the gospel, and its anathemas stand unreversed. The divide remains.

Live questions

The Reformation is not ancient history. Its questions are live in every pulpit and pew. Is the righteousness that justifies me mine or Christ’s? Is my assurance grounded in my performance or in his finished work? Is Scripture the final authority, or does cultural consensus overrule it? Every generation must answer for itself, and the Reformation shows what the answers cost and what they are worth.

For reflection

How would you explain Luther’s discovery in Romans 1:17 to a friend? Which of the five solas is most under pressure in your setting? Where might God be calling you to “stand” on his word at some cost?

6.title: Post-Reformation and Puritanism (AD 1560–1700)
6.essay:
The generation after the Reformers faced a different challenge: not breaking from Rome, but building churches that were doctrinally sound, spiritually alive and practically ordered, able to carry the Reformation across generations. It is one thing to recover the gospel and another to embody it in communities of real people.

Heidelberg

The Heidelberg Catechism, written in 1563 under Elector Frederick III, is the most beloved of the Reformed confessions. Its first question — “What is your only comfort in life and in death?” — and its answer, “That I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ”, may be the most pastorally powerful words in the history of catechesis. The catechism is built around three themes: our misery, our deliverance and our gratitude. Guilt, grace and gratitude is the shape of the Christian life, and the catechism has taught it to ordinary believers ever since.

Westminster

The Westminster Assembly (1643–1649), called by Parliament during the English Civil War, produced the most influential set of Reformed confessional documents in history: the Westminster Confession of Faith, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and the Directory for Public Worship. They were the work of 121 ministers and some thirty laymen, meeting for years under the pressure of war. The Shorter Catechism’s first answer — “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever” — has been called one of the greatest sentences in the English language. These documents have been the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian and Reformed churches around the world for nearly four centuries.

The period also developed and systematised covenant theology: the covenant of redemption, the eternal agreement within the Trinity to redeem the elect; the covenant of works with Adam in the garden; and the covenant of grace with sinners through Christ. Together they offer a way of reading the whole Bible as one story of redemption — not imposed on Scripture but discovered in it. The Covenant Theology study explores this.

The Puritans

The English Puritans, who wanted to “purify” the Church of England of its remaining Catholic elements, produced a generation of preachers and writers whose work remains among the richest in Christian history: John Owen on the Holy Spirit, Richard Baxter on pastoral ministry, John Bunyan on the pilgrim life, Thomas Watson on the catechism. Their learning was vast, their output prodigious, and their concern for the ordinary believer’s walk with God unmatched.

They are often caricatured as grim moralists. The reality is close to the opposite. Their pastoral tradition — from Baxter’s house-to-house visiting in Kidderminster to Owen’s meditations on communion with God — burns with concern for the spiritual health of ordinary people. They wrote about assurance, the mortification of sin, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, marriage and family, with a warmth seldom matched. For all their failures — some legalism, and the political zeal of some — they produced communities of great spiritual depth. Kitchens, counting houses and parliament chambers were as much arenas of God’s glory as the Sunday pulpit. The modern divide between sacred and secular would have baffled a Puritan.

John Owen

John Owen (1616–1683) was the greatest English theologian of the seventeenth century, perhaps of any century. His works fill twenty-four volumes and range across the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, justification, the priesthood of Christ and the mortification of sin. His treatises on sin and holiness are not academic exercises but battle reports from a man who fought the battles he described. His Communion with God, a meditation on the believer’s fellowship with each person of the Trinity, is as tender as any devotional and as rigorous as any systematic theology.

John Bunyan

Bunyan (1628–1688) was a tinker, a mender of pots and pans, who spent twelve years in Bedford jail for preaching without a licence and used the time to begin what was for centuries one of the most widely read books in English after the Bible. The Pilgrim’s Progress follows Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, through the Slough of Despond, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Vanity Fair and Doubting Castle. It is an allegory, but also a map of the Christian life so accurate that readers in every culture recognise themselves in it. Bunyan knew the Slough of Despond and Doubting Castle personally. And in his story it is at the cross — not through Christian’s effort, sincerity or persistence — that the burden falls off. That is Bunyan’s gospel, and the only gospel.

The Great Ejection

On 24 August 1662, St Bartholomew’s Day, some two thousand Puritan ministers were ejected from their parishes for refusing to conform to the restored Prayer Book and episcopacy. They lost homes, incomes and pulpits; many were banned from preaching within five miles of their former parishes. They suffered with a dignity that shamed the authorities. Richard Baxter, whose The Reformed Pastor (1656) was already the most searching pastoral manual in the language, was barred from Kidderminster and ministered wherever he could. The ejected ministers are the fathers of English Nonconformity — Congregationalists, Presbyterians and Baptists who would not let the state dictate their worship or silence their preaching.

An antidote

The Puritans are the best antidote to superficial Christianity. In an age of ten-minute devotionals and inspirational soundbites, they call us to slow down, go deep and think hard. Owen’s The Mortification of Sin, Baxter’s The Reformed Pastor, Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress and Watson’s A Body of Divinity are not easy reads, but they are nourishing, and they were written for working people, not specialists. Whoever reads Owen carefully will know his own heart better, know his Saviour better, and love him more.

For reflection

How would you answer the Heidelberg Catechism’s first question in your own words? What caricature of the Puritans have you held, and what does this chapter correct? Choose one Puritan book to read slowly this year.

7.title: The Great Awakenings (AD 1700–1850)
7.essay:
By the early eighteenth century the spiritual temperature of the English-speaking world had dropped sharply. The Puritan fires had cooled, and the church was marked by formalism, rationalism and a moralism that put respectability in the place of new birth. Then in the 1730s God moved — in Northampton, Massachusetts, in the fields of England, among the miners of Wales — with a power that astonished even those who experienced it.

A sovereign work

The Great Awakening was not a human programme but a sovereign act of grace that swept tens of thousands into the kingdom and reshaped the religious landscape of the Western world. Before it, church membership in America was declining, the Lord’s Supper was rarely kept, and many sermons had become moral essays. After it, tens of thousands had been truly converted, churches had been planted, Princeton had been founded to train ministers, and American Christianity had changed for good. It did not produce a utopia, but real Christians, with real sins and real battles ahead. It was real.

Jonathan Edwards

Jonathan Edwards, the most important theologian in American history and one of the greatest in the church’s history, saw a revival in Northampton in 1734–35, marked by deep conviction of sin, genuine conversion and lasting change; hundreds were converted in a small New England town. His sermon “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” (1741) is remembered for its vivid picture of divine wrath, usually without its context. Edwards preached in the spirit of Paul’s words, “Note then the kindness and the severity of God” (Romans 11:22). The wrath is real, and so is the mercy.

He spent the rest of his life studying revival — what it is, how to test it, what it produces. His Religious Affections remains the most important work on discerning genuine spiritual experience. Its central insight is that the test of true revival is not the intensity of emotion but the quality of fruit. Does the awakened person love God and other believers? Do they have a deeper sense of their own sin and of Christ’s sufficiency? Is there lasting change? Genuine revival always produces humility; false revival produces pride, the sense of having had an experience others lack. Not every crowd around a preacher is the Spirit’s work.

George Whitefield

George Whitefield (1714–1770) crossed the Atlantic thirteen times and preached to crowds of tens of thousands in the open fields of England and America — perhaps to more people than anyone before amplification. Benjamin Franklin, no Christian, attended his Philadelphia meetings and calculated that his voice could reach thirty thousand people in the open air. The actor David Garrick is said to have remarked that Whitefield could make an audience weep just by the way he said “Mesopotamia”.

What made him extraordinary was not only his voice but his gospel: the absolute necessity of the new birth, the free offer of Christ to every sinner, the grace that saves without any merit. He wept as he preached, over sinners, over grace and over the cross. He was also, to the church’s shame, a slaveholder who campaigned for slavery to be permitted in Georgia — a sober reminder that God’s greatest servants can be gravely wrong.

The Wesleys

John Wesley’s heart was “strangely warmed” at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, in 1738, as Luther’s preface to Romans was read aloud. He went on to ride a quarter of a million miles on horseback, preach some forty thousand sermons and organise the Methodist movement, which became for a time the largest Protestant denomination in America. Charles wrote over six thousand hymns, including “And Can It Be”, “O for a Thousand Tongues” and “Hark! the Herald Angels Sing”, teaching theology to a generation through song. Wesley’s Arminianism and Whitefield’s Calvinism made election the defining controversy of the revival, yet each recognised in the other a genuine love for God and for souls.

William Carey

William Carey (1761–1834) was a Northamptonshire shoemaker who taught himself Greek, Latin and Hebrew. His 1792 Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens launched the modern missionary movement. When he raised the idea at a ministers’ meeting, he was reportedly told, “Sit down, young man. When God wants to convert the heathen, he will do it without your help.” He sailed for India anyway. Forty years later, never having returned to England and having buried his first wife there, he and his colleagues had translated the whole Bible into Bengali and parts of it into many other languages. Carey understood that God’s sovereignty in salvation does not remove human means but demands them, and that the most urgent means is taking the gospel where it has not gone. His motto: expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.

Spurgeon

The revival’s fruit reached into the next century in Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834–1892), who began preaching at sixteen and in his early twenties was filling the largest halls in London. The Metropolitan Tabernacle held six thousand, with thousands more turned away. He preached from brief notes with a clarity that made deep theology accessible to coal miners and duchesses alike, and his sermons fill sixty-three volumes. He was also a man of sorrows — severe depression, gout and Bright’s disease — and in the Downgrade Controversy he fought almost alone against the liberalism entering the Baptist Union, at great cost to his health. He died at fifty-seven, worn out. His sermons live on: Calvinist, evangelistic and full of Christ.

Prayer and revival

The Awakenings teach what the church constantly forgets: revival is not a technique. It cannot be manufactured by the right programme, music, preacher or atmosphere. It is the Spirit moving where he wills. That does not make means irrelevant; it makes them desperately dependent on prayer. The great revivals were bathed in it — the Moravian prayer watch at Herrnhut, begun in 1727, which ran for a hundred years, and the concerts of prayer Edwards urged, which helped prepare for the revivals and missionary movement of the 1790s.

The Western church needs what the Awakenings brought: not a better programme but a genuine work of the Spirit. We cannot produce revival. But we can be praying, Scripture-saturated, gospel-proclaiming communities, through which God has always chosen to work.

For reflection

Why is it dangerous to treat revival as a technique? How would Edwards’s tests of true revival apply to your own experience? What does Whitefield’s failure on slavery teach about our blind spots? How could you pray more specifically for God to awaken his church?

8.title: The Modern Church (AD 1850–Present)
8.essay:
The modern period of church history is at once the most geographically expansive and the most theologically confused in the history of Christianity.

A world church

The gospel has reached every nation on earth. The great missionary century of the 1800s, followed by the explosion of the church in Africa, Asia and Latin America in the 1900s, has made Christianity truly and irreversibly a world faith, with its centre of gravity now in the Global South. In 1900 the great majority of the world’s Christians lived in Europe and North America; today only about a third do. Nigeria has more practising Anglicans than the Church of England. South Korea has become one of the largest missionary-sending nations on earth. The church in China, grown under communist persecution to tens of millions, is among the fastest-growing in the world.

The church of the Global South is in many ways more theologically conservative, more evangelistically fervent and more willing to suffer for the gospel than its Western counterpart. It is the most important story in modern Christianity, and the Western church has largely missed it. The Spirit goes where he wills.

The battle for Scripture

At the same time, the modern period has seen the most sustained assault on biblical Christianity since the Arian controversy. Nineteenth-century liberal Protestantism tried to reconcile Christianity with modern thought — Enlightenment rationalism, historical criticism and later Darwinian evolution — by stripping it of the miraculous. Schleiermacher, Ritschl and Harnack produced a Christianity centred on religious feeling and ethical ideals rather than the risen Christ and the atoning cross. The Bible became a human document, the miracles legends, the resurrection a symbol.

The Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy of the early twentieth century was the decisive battle. J. Gresham Machen of Princeton contended for the historic faith against the liberalising of the mainline denominations. He lost the denomination — he was deposed from its ministry in 1936 — but preserved the gospel for those who came after him. The mainline churches that gave way to liberalism have since declined toward institutional collapse; the churches that held the word have grown, or at least endured.

The Confessing Church

The German church under National Socialism is the most sobering case study of the century. Most German Protestant churches, seduced by nationalism and intimidated by power, accommodated themselves to the Nazi regime, putting racial ideology where the gospel should be. The Confessing Church — Karl Barth, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Martin Niemöller — refused, and in the Barmen Declaration of 1934 confessed: “Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God which we have to hear and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death.” Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945, two weeks before the camp was liberated. He was thirty-nine. The cost of faithfulness can be everything. It is always worth it.

Lloyd-Jones

Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899–1981) was a Welsh physician who became the greatest Reformed preacher of the twentieth century. His ministry at Westminster Chapel in London from 1938 to 1968 shaped a generation of ministers across the English-speaking world, and his expository series on Romans (fourteen years) and Ephesians (eight) are monuments of sustained exposition. More than anyone, “the Doctor” led the recovery of Reformed theology in Britain — through his preaching, the Puritan and Westminster Conferences he helped found, and his encouragement of the Banner of Truth Trust’s republication of Puritan works. He believed the church’s greatest need is always the same: real preaching that brings a sense of the presence and glory of God.

Schaeffer

Francis Schaeffer (1912–1984) founded L’Abri in the Swiss Alps in 1955 and for three decades welcomed the broken, the searching and the intellectually troubled — hippies and philosophers, artists and scientists — who asked whether Christianity could be true in a world where truth itself was under attack. His answer was not a leap in the dark but a reasoned, historically grounded yes. The God Who Is There, Escape from Reason and He Is There and He Is Not Silent gave a generation of evangelicals tools to engage secular culture without surrendering to it, and his later work on abortion helped launch the pro-life movement. He showed that Reformed orthodoxy and cultural engagement are allies, not enemies.

Faithfulness over relevance

The church in the West today faces pressures the early church would recognise: a culture increasingly hostile to Christian claims, a sexual ethic directly opposed to Scripture, and the temptation to buy acceptance by abandoning distinctive truth. The modern period teaches a lesson each generation must relearn. The church is most useful to its culture when it is most distinct from it, and least useful when most similar. Liberal Protestantism sought relevance and produced emptiness. Faithfulness is not a growth strategy; it is obedience. But it is also, consistently and providentially, the condition under which God builds his church.

The Western church is losing cultural power and prestige faster than anyone imagined fifty years ago. That is not necessarily bad news. The church has always been most spiritually alive when it had least to lose. The early church had no power. The Reformers were outlaws. The Puritans were ejected. The Confessing Church was illegal. Each time, losing respectability drove the church back to its only real resources: the word of God, the Spirit of God and the promise of the one who builds. We are in good company.

The Builder has not retired

Two thousand years of history come down to one conviction: Jesus will build his church. Roman persecution, Arian heresy, medieval corruption, Enlightenment rationalism, communist totalitarianism and postmodern deconstruction have all failed to destroy it — not because the church is resilient, but because the Builder is sovereign. He is “the living one”, who says, “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). The gates of hell are still pushing. The promise still holds.

For reflection

What does the growth of the church in the Global South teach Western Christians? Where are you tempted to choose relevance over faithfulness? What does the Barmen Declaration ask of you? How does Revelation 1:18 steady you as you look at the church today?
